passage: I'm Kashish. For about a month I ran to Mummy every time Sachin did anything. "Mummy, he looked at me!" "Mummy, he took my eraser!" I wanted him to get punished. One evening Mummy sighed and said, "Kashish, I can't tell which times matter." That stung. I thought about it while brushing my teeth. The next day Sachin used my sharpener, and I said, "Please ask first." He said okay, and that was that. Then he hid my shoe near the stairs, which was dangerous, and that time I did tell Mummy. She came at once. I am learning to tell the difference.

qa.q: What did Kashish say to Sachin when he used the sharpener?
Why did Kashish run to Mummy about every small thing?
qa.a: Kashish wanted Sachin to get punished.

qa.q: How can Kashish decide when to tell Mummy and when to handle it alone?
qa.a: Kashish can handle small things by speaking to Sachin and tell Mummy when someone could really get hurt, as with the hidden shoe near the stairs.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel about hearing so many small complaints?
qa.a: Mummy sighed and said she could not tell which times mattered, so she probably found it hard to know when to step in.

grounding: A child who tattles constantly learns to handle small issues alone and tell adults about real harm.

passage:
Tushar ran to Aai every time his little brother Nitin did anything. "Aai, he took my marbles!" "Aai, he's making faces!" "Aai, he stepped on my shadow!"
Each time he hoped Nitin would get a scolding.
One evening, while drawing water at the village well, Aai sighed. "Tushar, I can't be your referee every minute. If it's small, try to sort it out yourselves. If someone's really hurt or in danger, come to me."
Next day Nitin took his marbles again. Tushar opened his mouth to shout for Aai, then stopped. "Nitin, give them back. You can use the red ones."
Nitin handed them over. Tushar felt oddly proud.

qa.q: What did Tushar complain about Nitin stepping on?
Why did Tushar keep running to Aai?
qa.a: He wanted Nitin to get punished, which made him feel like he was winning.

qa.q: What did Tushar do differently the next day?
qa.a: He solved the marble problem himself by asking Nitin to give them back and offering the red ones.

qa.q: How might Aai see all the tattling?
qa.a: Aai seems tired of being a referee and wants Tushar to handle small things himself.

grounding: A boy tattles on his brother constantly, hoping he will be punished; after his mother explains when to tell, he solves a small problem himself.

passage:
In their London flat, Emeka kept reporting his little brother Obi to Mrs Chen, their after-school babysitter. "He's eating my crisps!" "He's looking at my tablet!"
Mrs Chen listened every time, then one afternoon she said, "Emeka, it's good to tell me when something's dangerous or someone's hurt. But not every little thing. Can you try sorting the small things with Obi first?"
Emeka thought about that. Next time Obi grabbed his crisps, he said, "Obi, those are mine. Ask first."
Obi handed the bag back. "Can I have one?"
"One," Emeka said.
Mrs Chen smiled from the kitchen.

qa.q: Why did Emeka keep reporting Obi to Mrs Chen?
qa.a: He wanted Obi to get in trouble, feeling a sense of fairness or power by telling on him.
That Emeka tell her about danger or someone being hurt, but try to sort small things with Obi first.

qa.q: How might Obi feel when Emeka talks to him directly?
qa.a: Obi seems to respond better, handing back the crisps and asking nicely for one.

grounding: A boy tattles constantly on his little brother to get him punished; the babysitter explains when telling is right, and he solves a small thing himself.
